questions.q: Match each validation check to what it tests.
pairs: That the data is of the right data type
That a number is between two limits
That something has been entered at all
That the data has the right number of characters
That the data follows a pattern, such as a postcode
questions.feedback: Each check stops a different kind of bad input. Naming the wrong one in an exam earns nothing however well it is explained.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: A program asks for a pupil's age in years. Which check makes sure 250 is rejected?
questions.feedback: 250 is a whole number, so a type check passes it. Only a range check knows it is impossible.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: A program asks for an email address. Which check makes sure it contains an @ and a full stop in the right places?
questions.feedback: A format check tests the pattern the data has to follow.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: State what is meant by validation.

markPoints.concept: checking that data entered is sensible or reasonable before it is accepted
markPoints.exemplar: Checking that data entered is sensible before it is accepted.

questions.example: Checking that the data entered is sensible and allowable before the program accepts it.
questions.paraphrase: Testing input against rules to make sure it is reasonable before it is used.
questions.feedback: Sensible, not correct: validation cannot tell whether an age of 15 is the learner's real age.
questions.misconception: Validation does not check that data is TRUE, only that it is possible.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: Explain why validation cannot guarantee that the data a user enters is correct.

markPoints.concept: validation only checks that the data is possible or sensible
markPoints.exemplar: Validation only checks that the data is possible.

markPoints.concept: a user can still enter something possible but untrue
accept: wrong|untrue|not true|false|lie|lies|lying|incorrect|not correct|not accurate|not their|not the real|made up|different|dishonest
markPoints.exemplar: So a user can still type a date of birth that is possible but not theirs.

questions.example: Validation only tests whether the data is possible: that it is a number, that it is in range, that it has the right shape. So a user can type a date of birth that passes every one of those checks and is still not their date of birth.
questions.paraphrase: The checks only establish that an entry is plausible, so somebody can supply something perfectly allowable that simply is not true.
questions.feedback: Possible is not the same as true. That distinction is the whole answer.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: A program asks for a pupil's name and the user presses Enter without typing anything. Which check catches this?
questions.feedback: Nothing was entered at all, so there is nothing for the other checks to look at.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: A program expects a whole number and the user types the word 'twelve'. Which check catches this?
questions.feedback: Something was entered, and it is in no sensible range, because it is not a number at all. The type is what is wrong.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: Explain why a program that asks for an age should use both a type check and a range check.

markPoints.concept: a type check only makes sure the entry is a number
accept: only|just|all it|does not|cannot|says nothing|no idea|no opinion|nothing about|no view
markPoints.exemplar: A type check only makes sure what was entered is a number.

markPoints.concept: so a number like 250 still has to be rejected for being impossible
markPoints.exemplar: So a range check is still needed, because 250 is a number and is not a possible age.

questions.example: A type check makes sure the entry is a number rather than text, but it has no opinion about which numbers are sensible. 250 and -7 both pass it, so a range check is needed as well to keep the value between limits an age could actually take.
questions.paraphrase: The first only establishes that a number was given; a second check is required because values such as 250 are numbers and still impossible ages.
questions.feedback: What a type check does not do, and what fills the gap.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 2: Type check

questions.q: A website requires a password of at least eight characters. Which check enforces this?
questions.feedback: How many characters there are is a length check. What they look like would be a format check.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 5: Format and length checks

questions.q: Match each entry to the check that would reject it.
pairs: An empty box where a name should be
A phone number with four digits
The word 'seven' where a quantity should be
questions.feedback: Each entry is wrong in a different way, and only the matching check notices.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 5: Format and length checks

questions.q: A program accepts only the words RED, AMBER and GREEN and rejects everything else. What is this called?
questions.feedback: A whitelist names what is allowed. A blacklist names what is not, and everything it has not thought of gets through.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 6: Whitelists and blacklists

questions.q: Explain why a whitelist is usually safer than a blacklist.

markPoints.concept: a whitelist allows only what is on it
markPoints.exemplar: A whitelist allows only the entries that are on it.

markPoints.concept: so anything the programmer did not think of is rejected rather than let through
accept: did not think of|not thought of|forgot|forgotten|new|unexpected|anything else|everything else|reject|rejected|blocked|refused|gets through|let through|slip
markPoints.exemplar: This means anything the programmer did not think of is rejected rather than let through.

questions.example: A whitelist allows only what is on it, so anything nobody thought of is refused by default. A blacklist has to name every bad entry in advance, and anything new — a misspelling, a trick nobody had seen — goes straight through.
questions.paraphrase: Because only listed entries are accepted, anything unforeseen is turned away, whereas a list of banned entries lets through everything it failed to anticipate.
questions.feedback: What each list decides, and what happens to the thing nobody predicted.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 1 — Security desk, station 6: Whitelists and blacklists
